label: text
text: To day the "salient point in the movements towards a settlement of the "strike" is that everything now hinges on the appointment by Canton of a delegation to negotiate with Hongkong's representatives.

label: text
text:
This morning the "Chinn Mail" was authoritatively informed that the departure of the Colony's mission, namely, the Hon. Sir Paul Chater, the Hon. Mr. Chow Shouson, the Hon. R. H. Kotewall, Mr. D. G. M. Bernard, will be fixed when, Canton, he announced the constitution of their body.
In the best informed circles it is considered that the report published of actual appointments is premature.
Interviewed by a vernacular paper representative at a private Cainese club last night, the spokesman of the second merchant mission "emphasised that he had come down to Hongkong on private business and in a purely personal capacity.

label: text
text: It is believed that the sailing of Messrs. Yeung Sai-ngaam and Kan Kim-shek from Canton was delayed from "Saturday" to yesterday owing to their being called to an important conference almost on the moment of embarking, though the discussions were stated to be of an informal nature.

label: text
text: In reply to a query he indicated that the prospects were rosy and that favourable intelligence would be available shortly.

label: text
text: Since the return of the first Canton, “unofficial”, delegation many steps have been taken behind the scenes.

label: text
text: The Hongkong Union of District Commercial Associations has written to Mr. Wong Ching-wai (chairman), Nationalist Provincial Government) outlining the recreation accorded the merchants here and laying stress on Hongkong's cordiality and friendliness.

label: text
text: This morning the "Wan Kiu Yato" published a cable from Canton, dated yesterday, to the effect that in connection with the ending of the strike, the labourers would select a delegate and the merchants one. The merchant nominee, however, would act strictly as a third party, using food offices as mediator and not participating in the actual deliberations.

label: text
text: Another noteworthy incident is the return to the Colony on Saturday of Dr. S. W. Ts'o who maintains that his trip to Canton was entirely in connection with private affairs. On Sunday he was one of those who met Messrs. Yeung and Kan at the Steamboat Co.'s wharf.

label: text
text: The merchant delegates also got in touch with the Kwangtung authorities and Mr. Wong is reported as having consulted Dr. C. C. Wu on the matter.

label: text
text:
This afternoon the China Mail was informed that a meeting of the delegates will be held at 4 p.m. at the Chinese Merchants' Club, when interesting developments were expected.
Confirmation has been obtained that the report of 'Canton's approvalments' was premature.
It is admitted that Messrs. Yeung and Kan are down here in connection with the negotiations. They were acting strictly as individuals—not even could their visit be described as "semi-official," it was stated—but in their personal capacities they were assisting in bringing matters to a head.
Chinese gentlemen who have received correspondence from members of the last delegation declare that most of the pioneering work is accomplished. Accordingly more definite information is anticipated.

Peking, Nov. 20.
A mandate issued accepts the resignation of Yen Kung-cho and approvals Kung Hsin-chan as acting Minister of Communications.
To-day's demonstration had a decidedly Communistic tendency, the students assembling being not only Kuomintangites but also a large number of workers, ricsha and other coolies. No national flags were observed; the students carrying the Canton flag and the workers had left.
The workers were all armed with stout sticks and accompanied by motor cars with doctor's and nurses. The demonstrators are now parading the streets and distributing pamphlets, demanding itter also the overthrow of Tuan Chi-juli, to kill Chu Shen and shoot all traitors; to dissolve the Tariff Conference and arm all the people for a popular revolution and a real national conference. So far there is no violence.

label: text
text: This afternoon's student demonstration for the purpose of receiving Lu Chung-lin's reply to demands made was not so largely attended as yesterday's gathering, probably because yesterday's display of violence aroused misgivings among the more timorous as to the likely consequences. "The immediate dissolution of the Tariff Conference" was one slogan prominently displayed this afternoon and the list of Tuan Chi-jui's alleged crimes against the people was posted up.

label: text
text: Pleading indisposition Lu Chung-lin refrained from attending the gathering and the students proceeded to discuss plans for the next move which threatens to include an attack on the “Chen Pao” on account of its anti-communistic tendencies.

label: text
text: In one of his essays, Tyndall refers to the use of imagination in matters scientific. In the absence of science during the Early and Middle Ages, the abuse of imagination was more obvious than its use. In those old times legends were more prized than facts.

label: text
text: The literal and somewhat prosaic tendency of the modern mind is apt-to treat with contempt, books which profess to deal with the lives of the Saints, filled as they are with narratives, which test to the uttermost the most credulous reader. It is overlooked that legends are not without value. They rest upon ideals. The Saints are the ideals of early ages incarnated in flesh and blood; and despite science, as patrons they have taken hold of the popular imagination in all countries, the legendary element notwithstanding.

label: paragraph_title
text: MISSIONARY ZEAL

label: text
text:
With St. Andrew we are on safe historical ground in the Gospels, which, however, deal only with his early career. Less prominent than Peter, his brother, Andrew appears a very earnest disciple and a member of what may be termed the inner circle. He seems to have been noted for his missionary zeal. After leaving Jerusalem he proceeded to the borderland of Mesopotamia, where he formed a church on the lines of the primitive one at Jerusalem, and to which Peter directed one of his epistles.
We next hear of St. Andrew at Sinope, where he met with considerable hostility. One day, while preaching in the market-place, great crowd, according to one account, "set upon him, and after jieasing and taunting the undaunted man to their hearts' content, finally ordered him to leave the city. He refused, and they attacked and maltreated him in the most fendish manner."

label: paragraph_title
text: CRUCIFIED CN A X.

label: text
text: Thinking their victim was dead, they cast him into a field outside the city boundary. Some of his converts found him, and carried him to a place of safety, where he soon recovered. In spite of the advice of his friends to leave the city, he remained in Sinope, where he became highly popular. Here he had a visit from his brother Peter, the last of their meetings.

label: text
text: St. Andrew's missionary zeal carried him over many lands. The scene of his final labours was in the province of Achaia. He was now about seventy years of age, and probably felt that his pilgrimage was drawing to a close. His lot in his new centre was not to be an easy one. The Roman Proconsul issued a decree calling upon all the people to join in offering up sacrifices to the heathen deities. St. Andrew refused obedience, and was flung into prison.

label: text
text: He was put upon his trial and condemned to death. Seven men, we are told, inflicted the lash, after which the old and feeble Saint was crucified. Further we are told that "instead of being nailed to the usual upright cross, a frame was constructed of two pieces of wood, which crossed each other in the centre thus X, and on this the apostle was tied with thin cord." As to where the body was interred tradition has different accounts. In the earlier part of the fourth century the body was removed by the Emperor Constantine to Constantinople with great ceremony, and reinterred in a cathedral which he had built in honour of the twelve apostles.

label: text
text: Now we come to St. Andrew's connection with Scotland: In this connection there is something of the -clusive Pimpernel about the Saint. The search for truth amid the conflicting accounts seems like looking for the proverbial needle in the proverbial maystack. Still, there seems agreement in the view that a few relics of St. Andrew were brought to Scotland in the year 369 by a plous Greek Christian named Regulus. THE CROSS IN THE AIR

label: paragraph_title
text: THE CROSS IN THE AIR.

label: text
text: Regulus appears to have been a successful missionary among the Picts, "the early inhabitants of Scotland." In the pages of Grub, who wrote the "Ecclesiastical History of Scotland," we find it slated that in a battle in which the Picts were surrounded by the army of the English king, the Pictish king vowed that if he escaped he would "dedicate the tenth part of his kingdom to St. Andrew. The same night the apostle appeared to the Pictish king, and promised him the victory. During the conflict on the morrow St. Andrew's Cross appeared in the air. The Picts were victorious and the English king was slain.

label: text
text: It is further said that the King built a church which was dedicated to St. Andrew, and endowed it with magnificent ornaments; and from that time the king's successors, and the Scots when the whole land became theirs, honoured St. Andrew as the patron saint of the kingdom!

label: paragraph_title
text: A POPULAR DEVICE:

label: text
text:
Whatever the origin of the veneration of St. Andrew, it had a remarkable bearing upon the claim of Kfng Edward of England to the sovereignty of Scotland. In the course of the proceedings at Rome, Pope Boniface laid claim to be Lord Paramount of Scotland on the ground put forth by the Scottish depicts that the country had been converted by the relics of St. Andrew, and that their Church had ever been subject to St. Peter, the brother of St Andrew.
The remarkable hold of St Andrew over the Scottish mind is shown in many ways. The coinage of Scotland in old times here the impress of the Saint. In the reign of James II. the Scottish Parliament directed that a new penny of gold be struck to be known as "The Lion," with the figure of a lion on the one side, and on the reverse the figure of St Andrew, closed in a side-case.
